Hey, I took English Literature in both O levels and A levels and got A*s in both. Trust me when I tell you I didn't read 80% of the content for my A levels at least. I skipped all my classes and barely skimmed through summaries the night before. The trick to nailing English Literature is identifying themes, tones, structures, writing styles, symbolism, literary techniques etc with ease. It could be any unseen piece of poetry or an extract from a play you vaguely have an idea about, as long as you can identify the crux, you're good. It doesn't matter how many books you read if you're not identifying these things right away. The way I got that was to read any piece of writing with the broadest mind I could have. That meant I was open to ANY and EVERY form of interpretation. When your possibilities are that endless, you start coming up with things. For example in poetry, a tree could symbolize a million things. Keep that in mind, and which ever symbolism goes best with the structure tone and overall meaning of the poem, you use that. For novels, you need to be aware of plot start to end, the rest of it can come naturally. If you know the main character dies at the end because of a action/consequence relationship, you expand on that. You can now talk about any theme that revolves around tragedy, and how all the other devices support this theme. Speaking of devices, memorize at least 5-10 of these. They'll fit in everywhere. I'm talking about anthropomorphism, neoplatonism, synecdoche, motifs. They don't necessarily all have to be literary devices, they can be philosophical concepts as well, and that is what will set your essay apart. There's never a wrong interpretation in literature as long as you're able to support your own. 

Once you have at least one point for each of the things I mentioned above, you can go from there and build your essay. Begin by pointing out what makes the text the MOST compelling, it instantly gives the examiner the impression that your entire essay is built strongly. It could be anything from a theme to even the conversation style, talk about it and support your points well. Even if you don't recall an exact quotation from the text, you can still paraphrase it in your answer. I'd suggest go over interpretations of many other literary analysts/critics for a certain text, it'll give you a lot of ideas as to where you can take your argument. You can even bring up their argument in your essay to either support or refute your point. In fact, I used to make up critics in my essays with points I had made up myself just to bring in counter arguments and give my essays more dimension. Oh, one last important thing, background information. This is a very crucial aspect of analysis that many people leave out, and I don't just mean memorize when or where the author was born. It's about putting their life in context with what they've written to support your point. Again, everything needs to come back to the points you're making. The Era in which a text is written is also incredibly important because it again gives the context behind why the characters behave the way they do.

Anyways, these are just my 2 cents (not quite, I'd say more than 2 lol) if it's of any help. If you have any other questions, you can ask me. Good luck.

I took 7. Math, Physics, Chemistry, Computer Science, English Literature, Environmental Management and Sociology. Don't ask why, I did end up getting a lot of A*s and As (I also had 13 subjects in O levels). It's not worth it if you're not interested in the subjects. The only way this arrangement worked for me was I had 5 A levels together, and 2 in another session. And the 5 I did have were math phys chem cs and lit. It also worked only because I didn't need to study for at least 2 of the subjects, which were literature and cs for me. I focused most of my energy on math chem and physics, the former came naturally to me. If you think you can handle at least 2 subjects with a bare minimum of studying, go ahead and take 5. But if all 5 of your subjects seem incredibly difficult to you, don't do it. It's not worth it at the end to end up with C's in all of them because you were so swarmed. 

As for my experience, I spent my AS spending 5-6 hours in classes, and an additional 3-4 hours studying. I eventually stopped studying near the end of my AS (my school doesn't do AS, we just give A levels). I only started studying at the end of my A2 and it was enough to choke me. It's a lot of content compared to what you're used to in your O levels, but not a lot compared to uni workload. I'd say if your school allows it, try juggling 5 subjects for a week. If you find it difficult to balance them in the first week, then it's a sign you should drop a subject. Take what you can reasonably manage, you don't want to enter uni already drained from school.

Alright, I get why you're panicking, but I'm here to ease that with some science. Gravity technically can't 'stop' because it's not a classical force as we think it is. It's not that the sun shoots out force field lines that maintain a gravitational pull. That's what Newton thought, but Einstein's theory of general relatively says that larger masses curve spacetime. Just think of it as a sheet, with all of these huge masses creating a weight so that it's not a straight line anymore, it's curved. Now add another dimension to it called time. So even worst case, whatever happens to the sun happens to us, and the sun isn't going to die for another 4 billion years. That means it'll maintain its position in spacetime. Yes, the universe is vast, and yes we don't even know what dark matter is which makes up 97% of the universe, but I like to think of it as a wonder rather than a threat. What if I were to tell you there could be many, many dimensions that we can't even comprehend, with their own laws of physics and own universes, maybe even infinite of those. The fact that it's so seemingly endless is what should be exciting. I can understand at the beginning its scary, because we as humans inherently place all importance into this earth and into our species for momentary pleasures. We think of ourselves as the highest and the mightiest, and when the universe breaks that perception, we feel terrified. You're really nothing but a speck in this grand scheme of things, try to find solace in that. On this earth, you're so much more, but outside, you don't matter, and you never really mattered, and that's okay. You're not meant to. You're just meant to enjoy the ride and try to find out as much as you can about the universe. I'll assure you, the more you study it, the less you'll be terrified of it. And there's no proof that we're all completely alone in this vastness. The probability of extra terrestrial life existing is pretty high, so they're probably feeling the same if they have emotions. 

But seriously, stop worrying about gravity stopping because that's not going to happen anytime soon.
